title: A hymn in Bilaval
hook: Bilaval holds Guru Arjan's song of shelter from the hot wind, sung after the danger has passed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bilaval, where Guru Nanak calls the Sultan sir and sings on gladly, and your line was morning joy. Did a small thank-you get said this morning? Day one thousand ninety-seven.

The storm blew all night. In the morning someone opens the front door and steps out to look: branches down, the street wet, the house still standing. Somebody puts the kettle on. Somebody laughs at nothing. Somebody cries, and it isn't sad crying. Relief has a sound, and it's closer to joy than to quiet. Today's hymn, in the raga we opened yesterday, sounds like that doorway after the storm. Today: a hymn in Bilaval.
screen: `THE STORM HAS PASSED.` → `RELIEF HAS A SOUND.` → `A HYMN THAT SOUNDS LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: First, the song. Bilaval holds hymns of Guru Arjan about shelter, and one of them, on ang eight nineteen, begins taatee vaao na lagaee: the hot wind doesn't touch the one in the refuge of the Supreme Lord. Earlier on this path we opened its pictures: the scorching wind, the refuge, the protective line drawn on four sides. Today, listen to something else: the tense. Second, look at the verbs. In paraphrase: I met the perfect Guru, who arranged all this. He gave the medicine of the Lord's Name. The Protector protected me and erased every illness. Grace came, says Nanak, and God became my helper. Met, gave, protected, erased, came. Nearly all of it is told as something that already happened. This isn't a plea shouted into the storm. It's a song sung after the wind has dropped. Third, the story people tell. Some Sikh tellers link Guru Arjan's Bilaval hymns of this kind to a time when his young son Hargobind fell ill and recovered. The hymn itself names no one, so hold that as tradition, not as something the text says. Fourth, why it sits in a raga of joy. Shelter and joy are two halves of one moment. Fear runs ahead of the danger; thanks runs behind it. When the hot wind passes, the next thing is to say so out loud. Guru Arjan set that relief in Bilaval, the raga tradition links with morning joy, so the thanks would be sung, not just felt. That's today's line: joy and shelter.
screen: `THE HOT WIND DOESN'T TOUCH.` · `MET, GAVE, PROTECTED, ERASED.` · `A STORY OF A SON WHO RECOVERED.` · `THANKS RUNS BEHIND THE DANGER.` · then, large: `JOY AND SHELTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Bilaval shabad, or remember a storm that passed. If you can, play a recording of taatee vaao na lagaee. Otherwise sit and breathe. Bring back one time something passed that you feared wouldn't: an illness, a bad night, a test result, a storm. Don't relive the fear. Go straight to the moment after, when it was over. Feel where the relief sits in the body now, in the chest, the shoulders, the face. Stay there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, as thanks. If you don't, let the relief be the whole of it. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Bilaval. Guru Arjan's song of shelter from the hot wind, told mostly in the past tense: the danger passed, and the thanks is sung in a raga of joy. Today's word.
Your line: joy and shelter. Today, say out loud to one person something you're glad got through: a recovery, a reconciliation, a near miss. Let the thanks be heard. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Bilaval shabad taatee vaao na lagaee is sung in kirtan and recited by Sikhs for protection and in thanks, at times of illness and recovery, before journeys and at births.

trapdoor: what you thought: a protection charm for hard times.
what it means: a hymn sung mostly in the past tense, thanks after the hot wind has passed, set in a raga of joy.

what a scholar hears: Bilaval Mahalla 5 (ang 819) moves from refuge to medicine to the Protector who erased every illness; tradition, not the text, ties hymns like it to the recovery of the young Hargobind.
